Independent F₄ Gram and n=4 orbit check
correctness.rationale: Dual distance at least 2 excludes exactly the zero columns. An admissible generator's projective column multiplicities give its class up to the projective-linear permutations: row operations give the projective action, and coordinate scaling and permutation account for column representatives and ordering. Hermitian Cauchy–Binet evaluates the Gram determinant as ∑_{i<j}m_i m_j modulo 2, because a pair from different projective classes contributes the norm 1 and a pair from the same class contributes zero. With t odd entries, the result is binom(t,2) modulo 2; among t=0,…,5 it is nonzero only at t=2,3, the even- and odd-length cases respectively. Nonsingularity also gives rank two. Flipping entries by +1 for even and −1 for odd entries is nonnegative, changes the length n to n+1, and maps parity weight 2 to 3. The odd side has d=(n+1)−max m′; d=1 would force multiplicities (n,1,0,0,0) up to order, of parity weight 1. The same update reverses the map and commutes with every projective permutation, proving the bijection on classes. The source convention 1≤k≤n−1 gives even n≥4 here. Independent arithmetic checked all 32 parity patterns and the 60 projective permutations, with a direct n=4 to 5 test of 50 admissible vectors and two orbits on each side. The supplied finite verifier was examined, not executed.
residual_risks: The finite replay is corroborative only. Classes are monomial-equivalence classes and the result is for the dimension-two identity only, not the companion dimension-three problem.

originality.rationale: The primary paper explicitly poses this exact all-even-length question. Its projective multiplicities and finite counts are prior; the supported new part is the parity involution proving the first identity on the stated equivalence classes for all even n≥4. No prior statement or implication supplying that involution or the resulting general identity was found in the checked sources.
residual_risks: The reviewed primary literature and catalogue checks are bounded. An independently discovered or differently phrased solution outside these sources is not ruled out.
